subtitle: The governance rules of the Internet Society as of June 1996.

tldr.problem: The Internet Society is a membership-based nonprofit. It needs documented rules for how its Board, officers, and members make decisions, hold meetings, and conduct business.
tldr.mechanism: The by-laws specify the composition and powers of the Board of Trustees (up to 20 members serving three-year terms), the roles of officers (Chairman, President, Treasurer, Secretary), membership classes (Organizational and Individual), voting rights, meeting procedures, and amendment rules.
tldr.outcome: These rules, as amended through June 1996, provide the legal framework for the Internet Society's governance. The RFC notes that the current version lives on the ISOC website.

today: RFC 2135 is an Informational RFC published in April 1997. It has not been obsoleted. The Internet Society continues to operate under these by-laws (with amendments). Readers should consult the current by-laws on the ISOC website (www.isoc.org) for any changes made since June 1996.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: RFC 2135 publishes the by-laws of the Internet Society as they stood in June 1996. The by-laws are formal governance rules describing the structure and powers of the organization. The RFC was published at the request of the IETF poisson working group and serves as a historical record. The document notes that readers should check the ISOC website (www.isoc.org) for the current version of the by-laws, as they may have been amended since June 1996.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rulebook that was printed in the Internet at a moment in time. The real, up-to-date rulebook is on the Internet Society's website.

sections.title: Board of Trustees and Officers
sections.content:
The Board of Trustees consists of not more than twenty Trustees, each serving a three-year term. Trustees must be Regular Individual Members of the Society. The Board elects Trustees, with at least four-fifths affirmative vote required for Board-appointed Trustees. The Board may elect additional Trustees by majority vote. The President serves as a non-voting ex-officio Trustee and is the Society's Chief Executive Officer, appointed by the Chairman with majority Board approval.

The organization requires four key officers: Chairman, President, Treasurer, and Secretary. Except for the President (who is appointed), officers are elected by majority Board vote for one-year renewable terms. The Chairman must be an elected Trustee (not appointed). No person may hold more than one office at a time. Officers receive no compensation except for the President and except for reimbursed expenses. The Board may appoint additional officers as needed.

The Board meets at least annually and may hold special meetings called by the Board, Executive Committee (if one exists), the Chairman, or the President. Notice must be given 30 days in advance (7 days for special meetings). Trustees may participate by telephone or electronic means and count as present. A majority of voting Trustees constitutes a quorum. Actions can also be taken by written consent of all Trustees without a meeting.
sections.plainLanguage: The Board runs the Society. The President manages day-to-day work. The Board meets at least once a year and decides big things by voting. More than half the Trustees have to be there to vote.

sections.title: Membership Classes
sections.content:
The Society has two main membership types: Organizational Members and Individual Members.

Organizational Members include: (1) Regular Organizational Members (organizations that contribute at least $10,000 per fiscal year, or a different amount the Board sets; nonprofits, educational institutions, and government agencies receive a 50% discount), and (2) Start-up Members (newly-formed organizations in their first three years of operation can join by contributing at least $1,000 per year with no discount).

Individual Members are: (1) Regular Individual Members (individuals contributing $35 per year, or a Board-set amount; only Regular Individual Members can be Trustees or vote), and (2) Student Members (full-time students contributing an annual amount set by the Board; Student Members are non-voting).

The by-laws also define special designations: Founding Members (for-profits or nonprofits that met high contribution thresholds by end of 1993 and remain Regular Members), and Pioneer Members (individuals who joined between June and December 1991). These designations carry prestige and may confer advisory roles or other recognition.
sections.plainLanguage: You can join as an organization by giving money, or as a person. Richer organizations have the same voting power as poor ones if you are both members. Only Regular members vote, not students.

sections.title: Administrative Rules
sections.content:
The principal office of the Internet Society is in the Metropolitan Washington, D.C. area, but the Board may establish other offices as needed. The Society's fiscal year follows the calendar year, and the official monetary unit is the U.S. dollar. English is the official language of the Society.

The Executive Committee, if established by four-fifths Board vote, can exercise most Board powers (except matters requiring a supermajority vote). The Executive Committee must keep minutes and report to the full Board. The Board may also establish other committees to facilitate activities, provided they do not take actions reserved for the Board or Executive Committee.

The Chairman is authorized to establish an Advisory Council consisting of representatives from each Founding Member and each Regular Organizational Member.

Amendment of the by-laws requires a four-fifths affirmative vote of the Board of Trustees at a meeting where notice of the proposed amendment was included in the meeting notice.
sections.plainLanguage: The office is in Washington, D.C. Money is counted in U.S. dollars. Big changes to the rules need almost all the Board to vote yes.

sections.title: Dissolution and External Relations
sections.content:
In the event of the Society's dissolution, its assets shall be distributed to a fund, foundation, or corporation organized under U.S. Internal Revenue Code Section 501(c)(3) (a tax-exempt nonprofit) or any successor section.

The Society may maintain liaison with other professional societies and similar organizations worldwide on activities that further the Society's objectives, on terms approved by the Board of Trustees.
sections.plainLanguage: If the Internet Society ever closes, its money goes to another charity. And the Society can work with other organizations if the Board agrees.
